## What you should be able to do tonight

- Justify each column in your bars table, including the two date columns, to someone who thinks one date is enough.
- Re-run the ingestion from an empty directory with one command and get an identical file.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Write qlib/store.py: a DuckDB database with three tables. `security` with an internal integer id, ticker, valid_from, valid_to. `bar_daily` with security_id, session_date, open, high, low, close, volume, and ingested_at. `corporate_action` with security_id, effective_date, action_type, factor, and ingested_at. Create them with explicit types and a primary key on each.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Write qlib/ingest.py: pull daily unadjusted bars for your universe via yfinance, map tickers to security ids, and insert. Make it idempotent, so running it twice does not double the rows. Use a session calendar from exchange_calendars to assert you have no bars on non-trading days.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The data store begins. qlib/store.py defines the schema and qlib/ingest.py fills it; every table carries both the date a fact refers to and the date you learned it, which is the constraint that makes point-in-time queries possible later rather than retrofitted.
:::

:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Why does bar_daily need an ingested_at column when a daily bar is never revised? Answer in terms of what you will want to know in March.
:::
